Am Bush: A shrub that passes for harmless hedge until something warm-blooded wanders close, then volleys toxin-filled seed pods into its hex. Armour is no help — the burst is a nerve gas, not a blow.
Giant Ant Lion: A wagon-sized larva that digs a funnel of loose sand and waits at the bottom. Whatever slides in meets crushing mandibles and a digestive venom that works while the victim is still struggling.
Army Ant: A moving carpet of biting insects treated as a single figure. Blades pass straight through the swarm; the only answers are fire, water, or frantic stomping while the stings mount.
Fire Ant: A red swarm whose stings burn out of all proportion to its size. Once it finds a gap in clothing it stays inside the armour, stinging every turn until the victim strips and sweeps it off.
Black Giant Ant Worker: The smallest caste of the black giant ants — a cat-sized forager that only fights when the nest is threatened. Alone it is a nuisance; a tunnel full of them is not.
Black Giant Ant Scout: A winged black giant ant that ranges ahead of the colony. Hard to swat in the air, it bites and flies home to fetch far worse company.
Black Giant Ant Soldier: A chitin-plated black giant ant bred for the colony's defence. Its bite shears flesh, and it never retreats while the nest stands.
Black Giant Ant Warrior Drone: The heaviest fighter of the black giant ants, all mandible and armour plate. It fights to the death wherever the queen's scent commands.
Black Giant Ant Queen: The bloated, immobile heart of a black giant ant colony. She cannot chase anyone, but every ant in the nest converges on whatever touches her.
Brown Giant Ant Warrior Drone: A yard-long fighting ant with jaws that punch through mail. It meets intruders head-on where its thick frontal chitin does the work.
Brown Giant Ant Worker: A dog-sized brown ant that would rather haul than fight — including hauling a downed enemy back to the nest as provisions. Being dragged off alive is the real danger.
Brown Giant Ant Queen: The egg-laying giant at the centre of a brown ant colony, too vast to move. Killing her kills the colony, which is exactly why the colony will not let anyone near.
Brown Giant Ant Scout: A flying brown giant ant, quick and evasive on the wing. Its bite is modest; the soldiers it summons are not.
Brown Giant Ant Soldier: A brown giant ant built for war, its head armoured like a shield boss. It holds tunnel mouths alone against armed parties.
Red Giant Ant Warrior Drone: A two-hex red ant the size of a pony, with a crushing bite and a venomous sting it swings into rear hexes or grapples. The most dangerous ant most people will ever see.
Red Giant Ant Worker: A two-hex red ant that forages in columns and takes livestock when it can. Even the labour caste of this species outmasses a warrior of most others.
Red Giant Ant Queen: A megahex-filling monster that founds and rules a red giant ant colony. She is a fortress of chitin surrounded by an army that dies for her gladly.
Titanic Ant Scout: A flying ant of the titanic breed, big as a dog and fast in the air. It exists to find prey and report it — being seen by one is the warning.
Titanic Ant Soldier: A horse-sized ant with frontal armour like a wall and a venomous rear-facing sting. Spears bounce off the front; nothing safe faces the back.
Apep: An immense serpent wrapped in its own unnatural darkness, which spills a hex beyond its body and blinds everyone inside it. It strikes from the black where no one strikes back well.
Arachne: A creature with a woman's shape above and a great spider's body below, hunting from webs strong enough to hold armoured prey. Cutting free takes strength most victims spend too late.
Archer Crab: A tide-pool crab that shoots a jet of sticky goo with startling accuracy before closing with its claws. The goo blinds and mires; the claws finish.
Bare Owl: A featherless-necked owl of unsettling intelligence and macabre habits. It is a minor threat in a fight and a major one to anything small, sleeping, or wounded.
Basilisk: A squat, ugly lizard whose gaze carries a natural Freeze spell to five megahexes. The bite is an afterthought; the stare wins the fight before it starts.
Banshee: A carnivorous bat named for its wail, all darting flight and needle teeth. It is nearly impossible to hit on the wing and hunts in shrieking flocks.
Small Bat: An ordinary insect-eating bat, dangerous to nothing bigger than a moth. It is listed because panicked people insist otherwise.
Vampire Bat: A blood-drinking bat that feeds on sleeping animals and the occasional sleeping person. The wound is trivial; what rides in the bite often is not.
Flying Fox: A fruit bat the size of a hawk, harmless unless cornered. Colonies roosting by the hundred can still empty an orchard overnight.
Black Bear: A forest bear that avoids people until food or cubs are involved. It hits with claw and jaw hard enough to end an argument in one exchange.
Brown Bear (Exceptional Male): A grizzly of unusual size, the kind hunters tell stories about instead of hunting. Its reach, hide, and temper make it a match for armed parties.
Drop Bear: A compact ambush predator that waits on branches and falls onto prey claws-first. Its victims rarely hear anything before the impact.
Giant Cave Bear: A bear grown to fill the cave it claims, tall as two men at the shoulder when it rears. It treats intruding torchlight as a challenge.
Polar Bear: A white bear of the ice that stalks prey across open floes — including human prey, which it hunts without hesitation. Cold, patient, and enormous.
Giant Beaver: A beaver the size of a boar, placid until its dam or kits are touched. Its bite fells trees, and its tail-slap knocks grown men off their feet.
Bloodtree: A carnivorous tree whose trailing vines snare passers-by, tangle their steps, and drain them where they stand. Rooted, but its reach is farther than it looks.
Giant Bombardier Beetle: A cart-sized beetle that sprays a scalding chemical blast behind itself when threatened. Attacking from the rear is the classic mistake.
Bison: A herd animal of the plains, placid at distance and an avalanche up close. A spooked herd is a natural disaster with hooves.
Bonnacon: A bull-like beast whose horns curl uselessly — its defence is a caustic spray from the other end that blisters everything in its wake as it flees.
Bull: A domestic bull: heavy, territorial, and faster than it looks. The gore is the danger; the fence is the safety equipment.
Cow: A domestic cow, dangerous mostly by weight and panic. A kick from one still cracks bones.
Ox: A draught ox bred for pulling, patient beyond reason. When that patience runs out it gores and kicks with the mass of a laden wagon.
Ruddy Bull: A red-hided monster of a bull that kicks with both hind legs and can gore two attackers in one sweep of its horns. Bred for war as much as for show.
Camel: A foul-tempered pack beast that bites at the front and kicks at everything else. Reliable in the desert, spiteful everywhere.
Beggar: A small scavenging canine that haunts camps and refuse heaps. It fights only when cornered, and badly.
Chupacabra: A hairless, hunched canine that drains the blood of penned livestock by night. It flees from people but leaves ugly work behind it.
Coyote: A lean opportunist canine, bolder than a fox and more patient than a wolf. Alone it takes vermin; in a pack it takes calves.
Small Domestic Dog: A lapdog or ratter. Its bite is trivial; its noise is the actual defence.
Medium Hunting Dog: A working hound bred to run down game and hold it at bay. A pack of them will hold a person just as readily.
Large Guard Dog: A heavy dog bred to stop intruders, with the jaw and nerve for the work. Trained pairs are worth more than a hired guard.
Demon Dog: A dog-shaped thing of ember and ash whose bite burns as it tears. Ordinary fur it has none; ordinary fear it causes plenty.
Fox: A small, clever canine that raids coops and traps. It is a threat to poultry and pride, nothing more.
Dire Wolf: A wolf half again the size it should be, with a bite to match. Packs of them empty valleys of livestock and worse.
Gray Wolf: The common wolf of forest and steppe, dangerous chiefly in numbers. A pack works a target with patience no single hunter can match.
Jackal: A scavenger canine that trails caravans and battles alike. It bites the fallen, not the standing.
Cannon Flower: A plant whose stalks fire hard seed tubes at anything moving within six megahexes. A stand of them holds a meadow like a battery holds a road.
Catoblepas: A heavy-bodied beast with a downcast head, an unnerving gaze that spoils attackers' aim, and breath that sickens at close range. It never hurries; it never needs to.
Chimera: A fused horror of lion, goat, and serpent: claws and flame ahead, a venomous snake-headed tail behind, and a hide that shrugs at spells. There is no safe side to stand on.
Cockatrice: A rooster-shaped reptile whose touch brings on the paralytic wasting called the Little Death. Small, absurd, and rightly feared.
Large Crabman: The full-grown form of the crab-folk, shell like plate and pincers that crack bone. Voiceless, it clicks its claws in warning exactly once.
Medium Crabman: A crabman not yet at full growth, already armoured and strong. They forage in groups, which is the problem.
Small Crabman: A newly land-worthy crabman, more shell than threat. It pinches hard and retreats to the water.
Monster Alligator: An alligator grown far past any natural span, capable of dragging a horse under. The death roll is not survivable without help.
Common Alligator: A river alligator that lies invisible at the waterline. It takes prey at the bank and rolls it under.
Common Crocodile: A crocodile of river and marsh that bites, drags under, and sweeps its tail through anything standing behind it. The bank is its trap, not its territory's edge.
Saltwater Crocodile: The largest true crocodile, at home in surf and estuary. It hits like a gate slamming and takes the victim to deep water.
Common Small Deer: A light deer of wood and field, defenceless except in flight. Its kick is a startled reflex, not a strategy.
Common Large Deer: A full-sized stag or elk. Outside the rut it flees; inside the rut it is an antlered lunatic with hooves.
Giant Deer: A deer the size of a draught horse, crowned with antlers wider than a door. Even predators wait for winter to weaken it first.
Diatryma: A flightless bird taller than a rider, with a beak like a pickaxe and a kick to match — and it can use both in the same turn. Fast, aggressive, and unbothered by spears.
Dipsa: A slime-covered snake so thin and pale it is nearly invisible, whose bite goes unnoticed until the venom lands a day's march later. The kill arrives before the diagnosis.
Dragon Hatchling: A dragon fresh from the shell, all instinct and sparks. Its flame is a candle next to its parents' — which is the thing to remember about where its parents are.
Baby Dragon: A dragon the size of a hound, already breathing usable fire. Bold, clumsy, and lethal to anything that underestimates the fire.
Young Dragon: A dragon at the awkward stage: big as a horse, flame that sets thatch alight, and judgement not yet grown into. The most reckless age of a very dangerous species.
Adult Dragon: A full dragon — sixty men's strength, a scholar's mind, wings, and a furnace throat that costs it real effort and repays the cost in ash. Negotiation is usually cheaper.
Elder Dragon: A dragon aged into something closer to geography than beast. Its flame unmakes buildings, its scales turn siege bolts, and its patience is the only reason anything nearby survives.
Young Adult Dragon: A dragon newly come into full flight and serious fire, eager to establish a territory. The eagerness is what makes it more dangerous than its elders.
Dragonet: A cat-sized dragon-relative that hoards shiny trinkets and spits stubby flames. Hard to catch, harder to convince to leave.
Air Elemental: A bound whirl of living wind that batters, deafens, and hurls debris. It has no body to cut — only weather to endure.
Stone Elemental: Animate rock in a walking shape, slow and inevitable. Its embrace cracks ribs like kindling, and blades ring off it uselessly.
Common Earth Elemental: A shambling mass of living soil and root. It smothers and crushes with the patience of the ground itself.
Fire Elemental: A striding bonfire that seeds fire hexes as it moves and flings fireballs from its own substance. Water is its only real argument.
Metal Elemental: The rarest and most vicious elemental, a moving mass of living metal. Its blows land like forge hammers and almost nothing marks it.
Ice Form: A water elemental frozen into jagged, walking ice. Only magic weapons bite it at all, and those only half as deep.
Steam Form: A water elemental boiled into scalding vapour. Armour holds the heat out for one turn, then cooks what it was protecting.
Water Form: A water elemental in its liquid shape, which flows over anyone standing in its element and drowns them there. On dry land it is merely patient.
Donkey: A stubborn small equine, more likely to plant its feet than fight. Its kick is a mule's lesson in miniature.
Light Horse: A swift saddle horse bred for speed over burden. It fights only by accident, at the end of a panicked run.
Pony: A compact, hardy horse for hills and children. Sure-footed, stubborn, and startlingly strong for its size.
Common Horse: The everyday working horse of farm and road. Its dangers are a rear hoof and its own panic.
Riding Horse: A trained saddle mount with manners and stamina. It kicks and tramples only when its rider or its nerves fail.
Draft Horse: A massive harness horse that moves loads smaller beasts cannot. Its kick carries all of that mass.
Warhorse: A horse trained to fight — biting, kicking, and trampling in the same turn on command. Half the value of a mounted knight is under the saddle.
Pegasus: A winged horse, shy of bridles and rare as honesty. It fights like a horse and escapes like a bird.
Mule: The working cross of horse and donkey: stronger than either's temper deserves. It kicks with deliberation, not panic.
Unicorn: A horned horse of deep woodland, fierce, fast, and impossible to tame by force. The horn hits hardest at the end of a charge.
Zebra: A striped wild equine that never accepted the saddle. It bites and kicks with a wild horse's full commitment.
Domestic Cat: A house cat. It cannot hurt an armoured person and will not accept that premise.
Cougar: A solitary ambush cat of crag and forest that drops on prey from above. Its grapple turns a bad first second into a worse rest of the fight.
Jaguar: A heavy jungle cat that kills with a skull bite and swims willingly after prey. In its wet, dark country it chooses every engagement.
Lion: The great social cat of the plains — the pride hunts as a unit and shares the arithmetic between claws and jaws. Lone travellers are exactly the sum it prefers.
Sabertooth: A shock-predator cat built around two dagger fangs, made to drag down beasts far bigger than itself. It grapples, anchors, and drives the fangs home.
Tiger: The largest of the striped cats, a solitary stalker of dense cover. It is faster and closer than anyone in its territory believes until proven.
Florasting: A hand-sized flying plant-thing armed with a venomous thorn, absurdly hard to swat. One is a curiosity; the cloud it belongs to is a hazard.
Florawing: A drifting cloud of ten or fifteen florastings moving as one. It settles over prey like weather and stings it into flight or collapse.
Flying Head: A glowing orange orb of a head that flies, grins, and lashes out with a barbed tongue. It bursts like a lanced boil at any solid blow — getting that blow in is the trick.
Forest Star: A star-shaped floor growth that fastens onto whatever steps on it and chews. It cannot chase, which is little comfort to the foot it has.
Giant Bullfrog (1-hex): A frog the size of a hunting dog that hauls wading prey under the surface. The bite is weak; the drowning is not.
Bullfrog: A common pond bullfrog. Its only weapon is its dinner-bell croak, listed here for completeness.
Giant Bullfrog (3-hex): A frog spanning three hexes, patient as the pond it rules. It swallows waterfowl whole and drags larger meals under to soften.
Giant Pacman Frog: A burrow-mouthed frog that is mostly an enormous hinged jaw. It engulfs prey in one gulp and works it down bite by bite.
Ghoul: A grave-haunting humanoid that eats the dead and sees perfectly in the dark. It fights with claws or scavenged weapons and prefers its meals unresisting.
Juvenile Gitaskog: A young lake-serpent already longer than a canoe. It tests boats the way pups test shoes.
Adult Gitaskog: A full-grown lake-serpent of enormous strength that swamps boats and takes swimmers. Deep water is its country, and it patrols.
Glyptodont: A living dome of bony plate on four legs, with a knobbed tail that swings like a mace at anything behind it. Cracking it open is siege work.
Clay Golem: A man-shape of raw clay animated to serve, wrapped in a magic that slides the eye past it. Its fists land with the weight of the riverbank it came from.
Golem Hound: A fired-clay hound animated as a tireless sentry. It does not eat, sleep, or bluff.
Parchment Golem: A servant folded from written pages that slices with paper edges and wraps around foes like a living rope, knitting itself as it fights. Fire reads it a final time.
Metal Golem: A towering figure of animate metal whose grip sears as it crushes. Short of a forge or a mountain, very little argues with it.
Wood Golem: A walking timber servant that senses living things across a wide radius and regrows any wound left unfinished. It floats, it patrols, and it burns — eventually.
Stone Golem: A granite figure animated for guardianship, sometimes carrying its maker's sight within it. It does not tire and does not miss its watch.
Gryphon: An eagle-lion that stoops from altitude onto horse-sized prey, striking beak, claw, and pounce together. It defends its high nest with all four of those things.
Harpy: A winged creature with a hag's face and a raptor's talons, filthy in habit and voice. It snatches, fouls, and screams — usually in that order.
Head Fly: A fly the size of a fist that goes for the face and will not be waved off. It cannot kill; it has ruined many people's aim at the worst moment.
Headless Man: A shambling human figure with no head at all, sensing the world in some other way — poorly, at its edges. What it wants is unclear, which is most of the horror.
Hippogriff: A crossed eagle-and-horse that flies with a raptor's temper and kicks with a horse's legs. It is tameable, barely, by the patient and the well-armoured.
Large Hydra: The elder growth of hydra, a rampart of necks and appetite. Each head strikes on its own, and the beast thinks better than anything with that many mouths should.
Hydra: A many-headed reptile that bites with every head in a single turn and speaks when it prefers cruelty with words. There is no flank where a head is not.
Hydret: The hydra's smaller three-headed cousin, necks weaving so wide its sides count as front. It is a hydra's danger at a market-fair size.
Hyena: A heavy-jawed pack scavenger that laughs while it works and hunts when scavenging is slow. Its bite cracks bones the big cats leave behind.
Ichneumon: A mongoose grown to six feet and utterly immune to venom and toxin — the fabled dragon-bane. It kills serpents of every size on principle.
Giant Jackalope: An antlered hare the size of a ram, absurd right up until the gore. It charges without warning and bounds away before the reply.
Fangaroo: A kangaroo-shaped predator with a carnivore's fangs where no fangs belong. It bounds in, bites deep, and is gone.
Miniature Kangaroo: A knee-high kangaroo of scrubland and burrow. Its kick is a warning, not a weapon.
Small Kangaroo (Wallaby): A wallaby — compact, quick, and inclined to leave. Cornered, it kicks harder than its size suggests.
Medium Kangaroo: A grown kangaroo that boxes and kicks when pressed. The tail-braced double kick has broken hunters' ribs.
Large Kangaroo: A man-tall kangaroo whose braced kick lands like a club swing. It will stand its ground and use it.
Kingowing: A crowned flying beast that rakes with claws and drives its head like a hammer, both in one pass. It rules whatever cliff it nests on.
Kraken: A ship-sized horror of tentacles and beak that takes vessels the way an octopus takes crabs. Every arm hunts on its own; the beak waits at the centre.
Common Leech: A swamp leech that fastens on unnoticed and drinks. Blunt force cannot harm what has no bones to break — salt and flame do.
Giant Leech: A leech the length of an arm that drains fast enough to stagger a grown man. It drops from reeds and overhangs onto warmth.
Komodo Dragon: A monitor lizard heavy as a man, with a septic, venomous bite. It follows wounded prey for days with total confidence.
Giant Monitor: A monitor lizard grown to horse length, sweeping its tail through legs and biting what falls. Its patience is reptile-cold.
Riding Lizard: A lizard bred and saddled as a mount in hot country. It is steady under a rider and still entirely willing to bite.
Saurian: A towering reptile of the deep wilds, a predator by mass alone. It walks through underbrush the way floods walk through fences.
Walker Lizard: A tall, striding lizard that runs down prey on two legs. It bites and kicks at speed and rarely commits to a long fight.
Long Lankin: A gaunt nine-foot figure that sees in the dark, sees the invisible, and cannot be fooled by illusion. Its long claws come through windows left open at night.
Mana Sponge: A drab, pulsing growth that drinks the magic out of the air — and out of spells, and out of wizards. It threatens no one and ruins everything.
Mandrake: A rooted plant whose man-shaped root screams when pulled, a sound that can stop a heart. Harvesting it is a profession with a short life expectancy.
Common Man o’ War: A drifting colony creature trailing curtains of stinging tentacles, blind to everything around it. It cannot aim, and does not need to.
Vampire Man o’ War: A floating stinger-colony that drifts deliberately toward warmth and treats every direction as its front. Its tentacles drain as well as burn.
Manticore: A lion-bodied creature with a man's face, a venomous sting, and a talent for mimicking voices to bait its ambushes. The voice calling for help is the trap.
Mauler: A squat horror that punches twice a turn and watches every direction at once. Its single great eye is the one soft thing on it.
Minipus: A hand-sized land octopus that swarms over a victim and clings. One is harmless; a wave of them is a smothering tide.
Moa: A flightless bird taller than a man, all leg and temper. Its kick and stabbing beak see off most predators — and most collectors.
Monopod: A one-legged humanoid that travels in prodigious bounces and lands, deliberately, on people. Between bounces it is oddly difficult to hurt.
Mothman: A silent, man-tall figure with vast black wings, seen near bridges and disasters. Whether it causes the calamity or merely attends it is the argument; the talons are not.
Baby Myrmecoleon: The larval stage of the ant-lion beast, a finger-length stinger in loose soil. Its danger is being one of hundreds.
6-inch Myrmecoleon: A myrmecoleon at its second growth, sting outpacing size. It hunts from a thumb-deep pit.
2-foot Myrmecoleon: A myrmecoleon grown to terrier size, biting and stinging in the same rush. Fields with their pits go unploughed.
4-foot Myrmecoleon: A myrmecoleon at its adolescent bulk, quick and armoured in patches. It takes goats, dogs, and the unwary shepherd's leg.
8-foot Myrmecoleon: The full-grown myrmecoleon, a lion-sized thing of mandible and sting. Its pit can swallow a rider, mount and all.
Ness: A long-necked lake beast that surfaces like a moving island, able to stretch its bite two hexes past its body. It is shy, until boats press the question.
Octopus: A soft-bodied sea hunter clever enough to wield three weapons at once in its arms. It camouflages, jets away, and remembers grudges.
Olgoi-khorkhoi: A fat red desert worm that kills with a jolt like a lightning spell, spits burning saliva, and bites what survives. The sands above its burrow look like all the other sands.
Ostrich: A tall flightless bird, fast as a horse and armed with a disemboweling kick. It does not want a fight; it finishes the ones offered.
Elephant: A grey colossus that reaches two hexes with its trunk and flattens what closes to one. Calm by preference, unstoppable by construction.
Hippopotamus: A river beast whose yawning bite crushes canoes and whose temper needs no provocation at all. It kills more travellers than any local predator.
Indricotherium: The largest walking beast known — a hornless rhinoceros tall as a watchtower. It fights nothing; it simply fails to notice what it destroys.
Mammoth: A woolly cold-country elephant with sweeping tusks and a shaggy hide like a wall hanging. Herds break through snow, fences, and battle lines with equal ease.
Pygmy Mammoth: An island-bred mammoth the size of a big ox, wool and tusks in miniature. Herds of them are stubborn, not tame.
Rhinoceros: A horned tank of a beast with poor eyesight and total commitment. It charges first and never asks the question the charge answered.
Greater Parrot: A large, sharp-witted parrot that mimics speech well enough to deceive and works simple latches with its beak. Its owners rarely know what it has repeated, or to whom.
Lesser Parrot: A small trainable parrot of bright feather and modest wit. Its bite is a pinch; its screech carries for miles.
Phoenix: A firebird that dies in flame and returns from its own ash. Fighting one is not dangerous so much as pointless.
Piranhakeet: A tiny parrot with a shark's appetite, dangerous only — and entirely — as a flock. A cloud of them strips a mule in minutes.
Pit Trap Plant: A pit lined with the plant's own digestive throat, roofed with false ground. Falling in is survivable; the hours afterward are the weapon.
Plocker: A round, furred forest animal kept sometimes as a pet. It bites gently and threatens nothing but rations.
Giant Praying Mantis: A mantis at horse scale with a strike quicker than a fencer's lunge. It holds perfectly still in the green until the reach is right.
Common Rat: The wharf and cellar rat. One is nothing; the swarm behind the wall is the actual tenant.
Giant Rat: A rat grown to spaniel size, bold in packs and foul of bite. Sewers and sieges breed them in numbers.
Common Roc: A raptor vast enough to carry off livestock, riding thermals no arrow reaches. Its stoop hits like falling masonry.
Giant Roc: A roc from which legends are correctly told — a bird that takes elephants as an eagle takes hares. Its wingbeats flatten camps; its attention flattens everything else.
Viridian Roc: A green-plumed roc of forested country, smaller than its giant kin and far more inclined to hunt people. In the canopy it is nearly invisible.
Scavenger Scarab: A heavy carrion beetle that swarms battlefields and boneyards. It prefers its meals still, and helps them get that way when pressed.
Small Scolopendra: A venomous centipede the length of a forearm, all speed and irritable fangs. Its bite burns for hours past the danger.
Large Scolopendra: A centipede at dog length whose venom leaves victims shaking with pain for hours. It flows over ground, wall, and ceiling at the same speed.
Giant Scolopendra: A centipede long as a wagon, striking from burrows with paired venomous fangs. Its bite drops livestock; the pain drops the rescuers' aim.
Common Scorpion: A palm-sized scorpion whose sting slips through boot seams as if armour were a suggestion. Painful always, lethal occasionally.
Large Scorpion: A scorpion at cat size with venom to match. It rattles its claws in warning exactly once.
Giant Scorpion: A scorpion the size of a pony: crushing claws forward, a killing sting arched overhead. The desert's most honest ambush.
Scum Bunny: A pond-scummed little beast that lurks camouflaged at the waterline. It bites ankles and vanishes into the murk.
Scuttle: A skittering blood-drinking vermin that slips into bedding and boots. Small enough to ignore, which is how it feeds.
Juvenile Sea Scorpion: A young sea scorpion, already armoured and armed at the size of a hound. Shallow-water waders find them the hard way.
Adult Sea Scorpion: A full-grown armoured sea scorpion that pins prey with its claws and shears it with its mouthparts. It rules the shallows it patrols.
Small Shadow Shark: A shark-shaped shadow that swims through the air and bites away vigour rather than flesh. Blades find nothing in it to cut.
Medium Shadow Shark: A grown shadow shark, circling the tired and the wounded. Each pass drains strength the victim cannot see leaving.
Large Shadow Shark: The largest of the shadow sharks, a darkness with a fin. It exhausts strong men to collapse in a handful of passes.
Shadow Skate: A small drifting shadow-creature, a skate-shaped patch of dark. It is less a fighter than a symptom that worse shadows are near.
Shadow Ray: A winged shadow with a whip tail that stings deep. It glides silent along walls and ceilings where torchlight fails.
Baboon: A dog-faced monkey that troops in disciplined bands and fights with slashing canines. The troop's males counterattack together, and hold grudges.
Chimpanzee: An ape of unsettling strength for its size, clever with tools and terrible in anger. Its grappling bite ends fights its screaming starts.
Gorilla: A great ape of highland forest, peaceable and immensely strong. Threat displays are a courtesy; the follow-through is not.
Great Ape: An ape beyond gorilla size, a hill of muscle with hands. Its open-handed blow lands like a beam falling.
Monkey: A quick, thieving monkey of canopy and rooftop. It bites when caught, which it rarely is.
Ourang-Au-Tan: A red-furred forest ape of deep, deliberate intelligence that trades gifts and keeps its own counsel. It fights rarely, reluctantly, and well.
Sinstoner: A vulture-sized corvid that carries a smooth stone aloft and drops it on prey with bombardier precision. Then it lands to peck through the results.
Brown Slime: A creeping brown ooze that smothers and slowly corrodes, indifferent to blades, bolts, and fire alike. Bare hands or strong acid — those are the options.
Silver Slime: A gleaming ooze that discharges a lightning jolt into whatever touches it. Only fire, acid, or explosion mark it at all.
Green Slime: A green ceiling-ooze that ignores ordinary weapons entirely. Fire burns it out — fire is the whole plan.
Red Slime: A rust-coloured ooze that shrugs off fire, heat, and cold, and eats metal to ruin in a minute's contact. Swords are both useless and consumed.
Slinker: A rat-monkey shape that flows through shadows with a thief's talent for not being seen. It steals food, shiny things, and sleep.
Common Constrictor: A modest constrictor snake that squeezes what it bites. It is a danger to poultry and to people who reach into the wrong hollow.
Large Constrictor: A python-class constrictor heavy enough to take a goat — or pin a person's arms while it works. Its coils tighten with every exhale.
Giant Constrictor: A serpent thick as a barrel that crushes armoured men, mail and all. Once the coils close, the fight is arithmetic.
Venomous Snake: A snake whose bite barely marks the skin and does not need to. The venom does the killing on its own schedule.
Giant Snapping Turtle: A snapper broad as a cart, with a beak that shears oars and hands alike. It waits buried in pond-mud with geological patience.
Monstrous Snapping Turtle: A snapping turtle mistaken, credibly, for an island. Its shell turns siege weapons and its bite dismantles boats.
Sphinx: A winged lion with a woman's face, learned, magical, and fond of fatal riddles. Its claws are the answer to answering badly.
Small Gate Spider: A hand-sized spider that weaves true magical gates into its webs and hunts through them. The web across the path connects to somewhere much worse.
Large Gate Spider: A gate spider at three feet of body, portalling between its woven doorways to strike from behind. Its lair is everywhere its webs are.
Giant Spider (Baby): A giant spider at foot-long size, venom already outrunning light armour. Nests hold dozens at this stage.
Giant Spider (Adult): A spider with a six-foot body whose bite slips through most armour and whose venom does the rest. Its silk holds warhorses.
Venomous Spider: A small spider whose entire threat is chemical. It gets inside armour, bites once, and the day changes.
Stone Beetle: A beetle armoured in what is functionally masonry. Cracking that carapace takes heavy tools and more time than its bite allows.
Stonemason: A small insect that chews building stone into meals and tunnels. It endangers no one directly — except everyone in the building above.
Domestic or Feral Pig: A farm pig or its feral cousin — heavier, faster, and meaner than town folk expect. The tusked feral gores; the tuskless one still flattens.
Wild Boar: A bristled forest boar that charges when wounded, cornered, or insufficiently entertained. Its gore opens legs like a plough opens turf.
Swordbird: A bird whose metallic feathers cut, stab, and — flung in fans of three — fly six hexes as blades. It is an armoury with wings and a grudge.
Tatzelwurm: A cat-faced alpine serpent that spits venom the length of a rope toss and bites with a venomed backup. Mountain folk wall their windows against it.
Tepes Briar: A briar hedge that grows explosive, poison-seeded melons and detonates them at passers-by. The hedge looks exactly like the safe kind.
Troll: A huge, misshapen humanoid that regenerates every wound as fast as it takes them — save burns. Without fire the fight simply starts over each turn.
Uncle Teeth: A long-necked river horror that strikes three hexes past its body, from any front hex, without warning. The name is the local joke; the empty fishing spots are not.
Vitranth: A living crystal formation with no front, no back, and spines in every direction. It does not chase; it is simply, painfully, where you put your hand.
Wampus Cat: A six-legged panther-thing that grapples with its forepaws and brings the remaining legs, tail, and teeth into the same turn. Escaping the grapple is the whole fight.
Berserker Wasp: A wasp that attacks anything moving in its territory, alone or in maddened dozens. Too small to hit, too angry to wait out.
Common Wasp: An ordinary stinging wasp. The sting is trivial unless the victim's blood disagrees — or the nest empties.
Giant Wasp: A wasp the size of a hunting dog with a sting like a spearhead and venom behind it. Its papery fortress nests hold squadrons.
Giant Wolverine: A wolverine at bear size with a temper the original never needed scaling. It attacks things it cannot eat purely on principle.
Wyvern: A two-legged dragon-cousin with a venomous tail sting guarding its blind side and a bite guarding the rest. It can use both in a turn, at a price it happily pays.
